drawing_organisms.alt: A hand-colored 1854 natural-history plate by Perrot: animals arranged across a pale staged ground with fine engraved linework.
drawing_organisms.caption: Perrot, 1854. Every generated plate aims for this engraved linework, muted wash and plain staged ground.
drawing_organisms.p1: Many of those 2.3 million tips are bacteria and archaea known only from DNA. Nobody has photographed “uncultured Crater Lake bacterium CL500-11”, so the plates are generated in the style of a 19th-century hand-colored lithograph like the one below.
drawing_organisms.p2: The pipeline is a fixed sequence of steps, with no agent deciding what to do next. It resolves the lineage, picks a living species to stand for the taxon, writes a prompt describing what that species looks like, generates an image and has a vision model score it. If the score fails, the prompt is tightened for one more try.

fifteen_attempts.alt: The fourteenth version: a wide, pale map of the tree with labeled nodes spread across the frame.
fifteen_attempts.caption_map: The fourteenth version, a map with the whole tree in view.
fifteen_attempts.html: Versions nine to thirteen went the other way. They built the tree in HTML and SVG, one clade at a time, with drag and zoom instead of a fixed picture. Names became readable, but the sense of distance from the origin was gone and the whole thing felt flat.
fifteen_attempts.webgl: It took fifteen versions to get here, each a fresh start rather than a revision of the last. The first eight used WebGL to draw every loaded branch at once, on a cream background borrowed from the graphic. Past a few hundred taxa, the drawing collapsed into a mat of dots, each the same few pixels wherever it sat.
fifteen_attempts.widest: The fourteenth was the widest of them. It showed everything, so nothing stood out. The fifteenth, [the one on the site now]({{current}}), does the opposite. It frames one taxon and what sits near it, fades the rest, and the taxon in the URL decides what’s on screen.

quota.p1: Generation runs across a chain of providers, tried in order, each with its own bounded retries. A provider that hits a limit it can’t retry past goes into cooldown and is skipped, so the next one takes the request. Text, images and vision each have their own chain.
quota.p2: There are two ways to run out. A daily allowance comes back the next day, and an empty balance only comes back when someone pays. I’d been treating both as a thirty-minute cooldown, so the site retried a spent account every half hour and told readers to “try again shortly” when only a top-up would help. The backend now tells the two apart.
quota.p3: A plate takes about a minute, much longer than a request should, so it’s generated in the background. The query returns whatever exists now, and a GraphQL subscription sends the finished plate when it’s ready.

the_backend.p1: Open Tree answers questions about subtrees. Ask it for a node and it returns what hangs below, but not what sits above, so the node arrives with no parent.
the_backend.p2: I stored nodes as they came, and “no parent” is also how the origin of life is stored. So after a fetch that started at *Panthera*, the site served that genus as the root of all life and grew the tree from there. It took a long time to trace, because the symptom showed up far from the cause. Now the first fetch of a node also fetches its lineage back to the origin, including the unnamed nodes in between, so every node is stored with a real parent and only the origin has none.
the_backend.p3: Everything is cached in MongoDB. Each node stores only its parent, and its children come from a reverse lookup. Lineages that share ancestors are often written at the same time, so two requests can race for the same node. That first happened when I emptied the database, and writes are idempotent upserts so the race does no harm.

the_picture.alt: A screen grab of a tree of life graphic: colored branches radiating from “$t(origin)” at the base, each tip ending in a painted organism.
the_picture.caption: The graphic I was aiming for. Around 250 tips, every one illustrated by hand.
the_picture.p1: I wanted every branch of life on one sheet, with something recognizable at the end of each branch, like a horse, a nautilus or a fly agaric.
the_picture.p2: The Open Tree of Life holds about 2.3 million tips. That’s too many to draw, illustrate or fetch, and almost every decision below comes from that number. So I stopped trying to draw the whole tree and started choosing what to show at any one point.

tuning_the_reviewer.p1: Scoring turned out to matter more than generating. For a long stretch every plate in the library, more than a hundred images, carried the same score: `overall 7, taxonMatch 7, pass true`. It was a hardcoded fallback. The vision provider had run out of credit, the call threw, and the pipeline filled in a pass instead of recording that no review had happened.
tuning_the_reviewer.p2: Three code paths could invent that pass, and none of them marked it as invented, so the database couldn’t tell a real review from a made-up one. A review that didn’t happen is now stored as no review. The scorer also has its own provider chain, so one spent account can’t silence it.
tuning_the_reviewer.p3: The rubric needed work too. It checked that the organism was the right one and matched the description it was drawn from, but never asked whether the anatomy was *possible*. A human with its head at an impossible angle, malformed fingers and a garbled caption still passed. Anatomy is now judged separately from identity, so the scorer can say “right species, broken body”.
tuning_the_reviewer.p4: I also took the bans out of the prompts, because naming a thing to forbid it tends to put it in the picture. A list reading “no insects, no mites” produced microbes drawn as mites, and a fallback description ending in “not a macroscopic animal” had been doing the same to the microbes in the library.

what_i_gave_up.one_taxon: The graphic shows all of its tips at once, illustrated, on a single sheet. The tree here shows one taxon at a time, with its lineage back to the origin and a sample of its neighbors.
what_i_gave_up.p2: Illustrations are made on demand, so most taxa have no plate until someone opens them and a provider has quota to spare. A taxon with many children shows a sample of them rather than all. The tree is assembled lazily from a cache in front of a public API, so the first visit to an unexplored clade is slow.
what_i_gave_up.p3: A visitor can still [start at the origin of life]({{current}}) and walk to any living species to see how far it sits from there.

where_it_started.p1: I started from [D3’s Tree of Life](https://observablehq.com/@d3/tree-of-life). It’s a radial dendrogram with curved links, tips labeled around the circumference and branch lengths that carry real distance. It shows the shape of a phylogeny and how far apart its members sit.
where_it_started.p2: It doesn’t show what any of them look like. Every tip is just a name. I wanted the shape and the creatures on the same page.
